hook: Four structures run **90% of all Python code**. Master these and every LLM library will feel familiar.

scenes.title: list = **List<T>**. tuple = a frozen one.
scenes.sub: Ordered sequences — one mutable, one not
scenes.narration: A Python list is C sharp's List of T — ordered, zero-indexed, growable, mixed types allowed. A tuple is the same thing but immutable: once created, never changed. Use lists for collections that evolve; tuples for fixed records — like a coordinate pair, or a row you don't want anyone, including yourself, mutating by accident.

cards.s: Mutable: append, insert, remove, sort. The default workhorse.
Immutable: fixed size, hashable, slightly faster. Fixed records.

scenes.narration: Compare: lists mutate — append, insert, remove, sort in place. Tuples are frozen — no changes, ever. Tuples are hashable, so they can be dict keys, and they signal intent: this record is complete. Everything else about them — indexing, slicing, iteration — is identical.

scenes.title: dict — **the** most-used structure in Python
scenes.sub: Hash map with literal syntax: {"key": value}
scenes.narration: The dictionary is Python's hash map — think Dictionary of string to object in C sharp, but with first-class syntax. Curly braces, key colon value. And here's why it matters for your future: every LLM API speaks JSON, and every JSON object becomes a dict in Python. You will live in dicts.

items.s: for key, value in config.items() — iterate pairs directly
config.get("temp", 0.5) returns 0.5 if the key is missing

scenes.narration: Three habits. One: lookup, insert, and delete are constant time. Two: iterate with dot items to get key-value pairs in one step. Three: use dot get with a default instead of square brackets when the key might be missing — square brackets on a missing key throws KeyError, and dot get just returns your default.

scenes.title: set = **HashSet<T>**, and it's instant
scenes.narration: A set is exactly C sharp's HashSet: unordered collection of unique items. Add a duplicate and it silently ignores it. Its superpower is membership testing — 'is this item in the set' is constant time, even with a million entries. Use it for deduplication and for 'have I seen this before' checks.

items.s: Pipe = union, & = intersection, - = difference — set algebra built in
The classic one-liner; order is lost (use dict.fromkeys to keep it)
Same as C# HashSet.Contains — even at 10 million items

scenes.narration: Sets come with algebra: pipe for union, ampersand for intersection, minus for difference. Dedupe a list by converting to set and back — though order disappears; use dict dot fromkeys if you need to preserve it. And remember: membership checks never slow down as the set grows.

scenes.title: Comprehensions = **LINQ in one line**
scenes.sub: [expr for x in items if cond]
scenes.narration: This is the feature that makes Python feel like magic. A comprehension transforms a collection in a single readable line — it's LINQ's select and where, fused. Square brackets make a list, curly braces make a set or dict. Once your eyes adjust, you'll read them as easily as a loop.

items.t: [m for m in models if "gpt" in m]
items.s: Where + Select combined — filter and transform in one pass
Dict comprehension: model name → its length

scenes.narration: Read left to right: expression, for, items, optional if. Uppercase every model name — that's select. Keep only names containing g-p-t, transformed — that's where plus select. And the dict version maps each name to its length. Same idea, three shapes. If a comprehension gets longer than one line, go back to a plain loop.

scenes.title: Slicing: **a[1:3]** means indexes 1 and 2
scenes.sub: Start inclusive, end exclusive — half-open, like .Substring
scenes.narration: Slicing pulls sub-ranges out of lists, tuples, and strings. The rule: start inclusive, end exclusive — exactly like C sharp's substring. a square bracket one colon three gives you elements at index one and two. Leave the start empty to begin at zero; leave the end empty to go to the finish; negative numbers count from the back.

items.s: First three · from index 2 on · last two — negatives count from the end
Unpacking: first gets items[0], rest gets everything else as a list
Swap without a temp variable — tuple packing behind the scenes

scenes.narration: The patterns you'll type daily: a colon three — first three. Two colon — everything from index two. Minus two colon — last two. Unpacking spreads a collection into names: first comma star rest — first gets one element, rest gets the remainder. And the famous swap: a comma b equals b comma a. No temp variable. Tuples make it work.

scenes.title: Time to write your own functions
scenes.next: Reel 4 · Functions — args, kwargs, decorators, generators

recap: list = mutable sequence, tuple = immutable record, dict = the JSON-shaped hash map
Comprehensions are LINQ in one line — [x for x in items if cond]
Slicing is half-open (start inclusive, end exclusive); unpacking + *rest replaces index plumbing

quiz.why: Slicing is half-open: index 1 is included, index 3 is excluded — so [20, 30].

quiz.q: How do you safely read a possibly-missing dict key with a default of 0.5?
quiz.why: .get(key, default) returns the default instead of raising KeyError. (The `or` trick fails when the stored value is legitimately falsy.)

quiz.q: Which comprehension uppercases every string in `models` that contains 'gpt'?
opts: [m.upper() for m in models if "gpt" in m]
[for m in models if "gpt" in m: m.upper()]
[m if "gpt" in m else m.upper() for m in models]
quiz.why: Read it left to right: expression, for, source, if-filter — exactly LINQ's Select+Where in one line.

code.title: The four structures + comprehensions in action
code.body:
models = ["gpt-4o", "claude-sonnet", "gpt-4o-mini", "llama-3"]

# list: mutable sequence
models.append("gemini-flash")
models.sort()

# tuple: immutable record
endpoint = ("api.openai.com", 443)   # host, port — fixed
host, port = endpoint                 # unpacked in one line

# dict: the structure of every LLM API response
response = {"model": "gpt-4o", "tokens": 42, "ok": True}
model = response.get("model", "unknown")
for key, value in response.items():
    print(f"  {key}: {value}")

# set: dedupe + instant membership
tags = list({"ai", "python", "ai", "rag"})   # → ['ai', 'python', 'rag']

# comprehension = LINQ in one line
gpts = [m.upper() for m in models if "gpt" in m]
lengths = {m: len(m) for m in models}

# slicing & unpacking
first, *rest = models
last_two = models[-2:]
annot: dict.fromkeys(items) also dedupes but preserves order — use it when order matters
Unpacking `host, port = endpoint` works because tuples unpack by position
Comprehensions over files: [line.strip() for line in open('f.txt')]

notes:
# Core Data Structures

## list & tuple
| | list `[1,2]` | tuple `(1,2)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mutable | ✅ append/insert/remove/sort | ❌ frozen |
| Hashable (usable as dict key) | ❌ | ✅ |
| Use for | evolving collections | fixed records |

## dict
- Hash map: `{"key": value}` — keys must be hashable (str, number, tuple).
- O(1) lookup/insert/delete.
- `d.get(k, default)` — safe read · `d.items()` — iterate pairs · `d.keys()` / `d.values()`.
- **Every JSON object becomes a dict** — this is the LLM-era structure.

## set
- Unordered unique items; O(1) membership.
- `|` union · `&` intersection · `-` difference.
- `list(set(x))` dedupes (order lost) · `dict.fromkeys(x)` dedupes, keeps order.

## Comprehensions
```python
[m.upper() for m in models]                 # select
[m for m in models if "gpt" in m]           # where
[m.upper() for m in models if "gpt" in m]   # both
{m: len(m) for m in models}                 # dict comp
```
> One line max — longer means go back to a loop.

## Slicing & unpacking
- `a[1:3]` = indexes 1,2 (half-open) · `a[:3]` · `a[-2:]` (last two).
- `first, *rest = items` · `a, b = b, a` (swap).
